svg.title: Transport processes
svg.desc: DIFFUSION: Net movement of particles of a gas or dissolved substance from higher to lower concentration. Particles move randomly; the overall movement is down the concentration gradient. No energy from respiration is required. Examples: oxygen and carbon dioxide in gas exchange; urea from cells into blood plasma. At equilibrium, particles still move but there is no net movement. FASTER DIFFUSION: Steeper gradient → greater net movement per second. Higher temperature → particles have more kinetic energy and move faster. Larger membrane area → more particles cross at once. Thinner barrier → shorter diffusion distance. Always connect the feature to why exchange becomes faster. OSMOSIS: Net movement of water molecules from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution, through a partially permeable membrane. The dilute side has more water molecules relative to solute. Water can cross; some dissolved substances cannot. No energy from respiration is needed. Water moves both ways; the arrow shows net movement. CELLS GAIN OR LOSE WATER: Dilute surroundings → water enters by osmosis. Plant: vacuole fills → turgid; the wall prevents bursting. Animal: may swell and burst. Concentrated surroundings → water leaves. Plant: becomes flaccid; severe loss can cause plasmolysis, where the membrane pulls from the wall. Animal: shrinks. ACTIVE TRANSPORT: Movement from lower to higher concentration, against the concentration gradient. Requires energy from respiration. Membrane transport proteins carry substances. Memory cue: moving uphill needs energy; the 'hill' represents concentration. Diffusion and osmosis go down gradients. Only osmosis is water-only. WHERE ACTIVE TRANSPORT HELPS: Root hair cells: absorb mineral ions even when soil concentration is lower than inside the cell. Ions are needed for healthy growth. Small intestine: absorbs sugars from a lower concentration in the gut into blood with a higher concentration. Sugars can be used in cell respiration. Many mitochondria support a high energy demand. OSMOSIS PRACTICAL: METHOD: Vary salt or sugar concentration; measure percentage mass change of plant tissue. Prepare equal-size potato cylinders; record initial masses. Use equal solution volumes, including distilled water. Keep tissue source, dimensions, time and temperature constant. Remove; blot consistently; measure final masses. Repeat each concentration and calculate means. Blotting removes surface liquid; use cutting tools safely. OSMOSIS PRACTICAL: RESULTS: % change = (final − initial) ÷ initial × 100. 2.50 g → 2.20 g: −0.30 ÷ 2.50 × 100 = −12%; water left. Positive → net gain; negative → net loss. Zero → no net movement, not no movement. Plot concentration on x; mean % change on y. Use a best-fit line/curve; its 0% crossing estimates balanced concentration. Rate = mass change ÷ time: 0.12 g ÷ 30 min = 0.004 g/min. Repeat; check anomalies; test more concentrations near zero.
